national.line: A kitten stuck in a car's engine bay in Tulare County, California, was lured out with tuna. Best tool in the toolbox.
A cat rescued from an overpass in Little Rock, Arkansas, has found a forever home. Nine lives, one great landing.
The aquarium in Branson, Missouri, set a world record by putting a giant Santa hat on an octopus. Eight arms, one festive head.
Roberta Flack told Clint Eastwood her song was too slow for his movie, and he made it a No. 1 hit anyway. Slow and steady wins.

pride.label: Yellowjacket of the Week
pride.line: Jackson Snyder is Lebanon High School's Yellowjacket of the Week for his work in athletics and the classroom. Sweet success, no sting.

pride.label: Streaming Milestone
pride.line: Marshfield native Kollin Bailey's Nashville country trio DEK of Hearts landed on Spotify's "All New Country" playlist and more than tripled its monthly listeners. Small-town sound, big-time numbers.

pride.label: Administrator of the Year
pride.line: Julie Routh, a Bolivar resident and principal at Sherwood Elementary in Springfield, was named MOSHAPE Administrator of the Year by Springfield Public Schools. That's a gold star for the principal.

pride.label: All-State
pride.line: Bolivar freshman Brielyn Hines placed seventh at state golf and earned all-state honors, while tennis players Jillian Horner took fourth in singles and Adelyn Seay and Kayla Goodman took fourth in doubles. Bolivar knows its way around a fairway and a court.

pride.label: $2 Million Milestone
pride.line: The Lake of the Ozarks Idiots Club has passed $2 million in help for local kids living in poverty, with the milestone dollar buying clothes for a Macks Creek student. Best kind of idiots.

pride.label: District Championship
pride.line: The Camdenton soccer team advanced to the district championship. Time to kick it up a notch.

pride.label: Grand Opening
pride.line: Eye of the Storm Massage held its grand opening and ribbon cutting at 290 East Broadway in Bolivar in October and joined the chamber as its newest member. Calm after the ribbon.

local.line: Laclede County agencies put warming shelters, food banks and addiction services on one shared list for people struggling this holiday season. One list beats ten phone calls.
Camden County landed one of Missouri's 131 new federal Opportunity Zones, which developers say could bring investment and affordable housing to the Camdenton area. Housing help may be on the way.
Ameren is asking people not to dump leaves into Lake of the Ozarks to protect water quality. Rake it, don't lake it.

music.line: Greylan James just scored his first Billboard Hot 100 hit with "Water at a Wedding" and is Billboard's Country Up-and-Comer for November. Somebody get him a bigger boat.
Cody Johnson released a special acoustic version of "Take Me Back (And Leave Me There)." Same heart, fewer amps.
The Country Music Hall of Fame and Museum opened a new Roger Miller exhibit. Come see the king of the road.
Garth Brooks added a pair of December shows in Minneapolis to his Blame It All On My Roots Tour. Friends in low places, now with mittens.
Wynonna Judd will receive the ASCAP Golden Note Award honoring her career. That voice earned every note.
Cody Jinks is promising a return to his country roots on his new album, "And, Again." Roots always grow back.
Johnny Owens is celebrating Buck Owens' Christmas legacy with "Santa Looked a Lot Like Daddy." Ho ho honky-tonk.

weird.line: Two rescued black bear cubs at the Oregon Zoo splashed around in a giant bubble bath with rubber duckies. Cleanest bears in the West.
Rescued bear cubs were released back into the Tennessee wilderness. Now they can bathe in a creek.
A mystery bald eagle was caught on camera exploring the famous Big Bear nest in California. Nobody gave it a key.
A fisherman from Menasha, Wisconsin, shattered a 76-year-old state record with a smallmouth bass caught on Green Bay. That fish story has paperwork.
A cow in a viral video gently asked a woman for a cuddle. Moo-ve over, golden retrievers.
A baby bear caught on camera caused a stir at a gas station. Probably wanted a snack and a restroom.
Police in Marshfield, Massachusetts, are warning drivers about a large cow that has been loose in the area for an entire day. Moo-ve over, please.
A raccoon, an opossum and a squirrel were caught on camera stealing candy from a Louisville library garage. Halloween leftovers never last.
An alligator went viral after strolling into a North Carolina bagel shop as if it were a customer. Hold the cream cheese.
A ball python was found in a trash can in a Glendale park. Somebody's taking out the wrong garbage.
Paddleboarders rescued a raccoon during heavy rain in Austin, Texas. Best ride that raccoon ever had.
A cop wrangled a loose alligator in a video of the day. Not in the training manual, probably.
A Florida man was spotted sucking on a pacifier outside a bank and said, "I don't need no money today." Honest and relaxed.

humor.line: Books began as clay tablets inscribed with cuneiform in the third millennium BCE, then moved on to papyrus. Hardcovers were literally hard.
The teddy bear was named after Theodore Roosevelt, who refused to shoot a bear on a hunting trip in 1902. The bear got the better end of that deal.
In 1973, New Jersey became the first state to allow girls to play Little League baseball. Girls came to play, and they stayed.
The word "notary" comes from "nota," a shorthand invented by Cicero's clerk to take down Cicero's speeches. Somebody had to keep up with that guy.
Dark chocolate has to have at least 35 percent cocoa solids, which makes this day the healthier cousin of Milk Chocolate with Almonds Day in July. Balanced diet, right?
Puns show up in Sumerian cuneiform and Egyptian and Mayan hieroglyphics. Dad jokes are older than dirt.
Tongue twisters lean on alliteration and rhyme, and Dr. Seuss's "Fox in Socks" is full of them. Try saying that five times fast.
Cappuccino is named for the Capuchin friars, whose reddish-brown hooded robes looked like the drink and whose name comes from the Italian word for hood. Coffee with a hood on.
Toy company MGA Entertainment created it, inspired by its Project Mc2 line, to get kids into science, technology, engineering, art and math. Even math gets a holiday.
Cooking tools tied to the pupusa were found at Joya de Ceren, a site buried by volcanic ash about 2,000 years ago. That's a very old dinner.
In Minsk, pianist Nikolai Panok once played for six hours without stopping for this day. His fingers earned a long nap.
Its creators, Thomas and Ruth Roy, say not to forget the sauerkraut and garlic. Keep mints handy.
Early British puddings were savory and sometimes cooked in an animal's stomach, long before sticky toffee came along. Dessert has come a long way.
Carl Sagan's 1980 series "Cosmos" became the most-watched PBS program of its time and won two Emmys. That show reached for the stars.
The fried chicken sandwich lets you eat fried chicken without greasy hands, and it took off after World War II. Napkins recommended anyway.
Scrapple was created by the Pennsylvania Dutch and goes by names like "pawnhaus," which means finely chopped. Don't ask, just eat.
Greek yogurt is thicker because it's strained to remove the whey, and most kinds carry live probiotics. Thick enough to stand a spoon in.
Area codes were devised by AT&T in the 1940s and fully rolled out with the North American Numbering Plan in 1947. Time to call someone out of your area.
Italian mathematician Luca Pacioli, born in 1445, wrote the first printed math book to include double-entry bookkeeping. Every accountant owes him a coffee.
The earliest cupcake-like recipe appeared in American Cookery in 1796, and the word "cupcake" first showed up in 1828. Tiny cakes, big history.
New York City temporarily renamed a Manhattan corner "123 Sesame Street" in 2009 for the show's 40th anniversary. Now that's a good address.
Singles' Day began at Nanjing University in China in 1993, when four dorm-mates decided to make being single more exciting, and the date has four ones. Four guys, one big idea.
Pocky looks like the number one, so Japan's Ezaki Glico celebrates it on 11/11, and the chocolate-free end is a handle to keep fingers clean. Smart snack.
National Metal Day lands on 11/11 as a nod to the amps in "This Is Spinal Tap" that go up to 11. Turn it up one more.
One story says a Manitowoc, Wisconsin, soda fountain owner named George Giffy served the dish only on Sundays, and that's how it got its name. Sunday's best.
Guinness World Records began after brewery boss Sir Hugh Beaver argued with friends over the fastest game bird and couldn't find the answer in any book. He wrote the book on settling arguments.
"Chicken Soup for the Soul" came out in 1993 with 101 inspirational stories and has sold over 11 million copies. That's a lot of soup.
Fancy rats and mice are show animals and pets, and their coats come in a wide variety of colors and patterns. Those whiskers deserve a spotlight.
Two downtown Los Angeles restaurants, Philippe's and Cole's, have long argued over who invented the French dip. Pick a side and dip.
Anchovies are the one pizza topping with almost no middle ground, so today the works come without them. Pizza night peace treaty.
Sadie Hawkins Day comes from the comic strip "Li'l Abner," which ran from 1934 to 1977, where 35-year-old Sadie still wasn't married. Her dad took matters into his own hands.
Almost nothing is known about where this day came from, so it may have started as a rumor. You didn't hear it from me.
Bread pudding dates to the 11th or 12th century, when it was a way to use up stale bread. Leftovers have always been a good idea.
